iterations.theme: Introduction, introducing the guest and the UCI paper on professional cyclists' nutrition

sections.subtitle: Welcome and introduction of the guest: who is Luka Batur?
sections.screenshot_description: Host Josip and guest Luka Batur sit at a table in the studio, with the title frame of episode #19 and the biciklizam_net channel logo on display.
sections.content:
The episode begins with an opening greeting from host **Josip**, who announces to viewers the guest **Luka Batur**, a nutritionist who appears on the channel for the third time, or the second time solo. Josip reminds viewers that Batur recently wrote a guide to nutrition for cyclists, and he lists the guide's topics as the role of fats, carbohydrates and proteins, how many carbohydrates to eat during a single ride, and what to eat before, during and after a ride. He encourages viewers to find the guide via the link in the episode description.

In the introduction the guest emphasizes that he is glad to take part in the conversation again and that all viewers already have an idea about the topic covered in the episode. Josip then asks Batur to introduce himself and explain what his credibility is based on. Batur admits that a question about his own credibility is uncomfortable, but he leaves it to clients and viewers to judge.

In his words, he earned a master's degree in nutrition at the **Faculty of Food Technology and Biotechnology of the University of Zagreb**, and he stresses extensive education in chemistry and knowledge of human metabolism as the foundation of his expertise in sports nutrition. He emphasizes that in practice athletes often consider an expert to be someone who has trained for a long time or has experience in sport, but he believes that scientifically grounded knowledge represents an additional level.

After university Batur worked at **KBC Zagreb**, and in parallel he works with athletes of various levels, from amateurs to professionals. Part of his work concerns people with diagnoses who need to adjust their diet. In recent years he has been actively involved in triathlon, which, as he says, allows him to see the issues from his own experience on two wheels.

Josip concludes at the end that the key lies in combining the scientific picture with practice, that is, in the ability to adapt scientific findings to what is feasible for athletes in the field. Batur agrees that science and practice are two different worlds that should be brought together, and he considers exactly that to be his strength.
entities: Faculty of Food Technology and Biotechnology of the University of Zagreb

sections.subtitle: Marginal gains: secrets of professional teams between science and detail
sections.screenshot_description: Guest Luka Batur talks about marginal gains, while a graphic showing the nutritional approach of professional teams appears on screen.
sections.content:
The conversation then moves to the work Batur has read and its importance. Batur states that it is the most extensive review of nutrition in professional cycling, and Josip reminds viewers that the researchers analyzed the period from **2016 to 2025**.

Batur explains that two years ago he attended a seminar in **Manchester**, where he had the opportunity to hear presentations from the researchers behind the papers being discussed today. He notes that such seminars are rare and that valuable information is obtained at a certain cost and by following the right sources.

When Josip asks how many secrets are guarded in professional cycling, Batur answers that it is probably a considerable number of pieces of information that teams do not share. He explains that teams compete with each other, so if someone discovers a new strategy, few will share it with the competition. As an example of a trivial detail, he says that sometimes even small pieces of information are not published.

Josip adds that professional bikes look very similar, meaning that top models in shops have no essential differences compared to professional ones. He concludes that the deciding factors are **micro details**: a combination of equipment, training, nutrition and, of course, talent. In his opinion, it is this set of small but collectively important factors that makes the difference between top athletes and others.

Batur agrees that teams do not employ only scientists, but also experts who are good practitioners. In his words, the research that is published was often created years before publication, so analyses, including those involving muscle sample analysis, are continuously carried out behind the scenes of professional sport.

sections.subtitle: Who stands behind the UCI paper: authors, teams, university and why it matters
sections.screenshot_description: Display of the cover or summary of the UCI paper with a note on the university and teams, alongside Luka Batur explaining the structure of the papers.
sections.content:
Josip then asks who the authors of the paper are, which teams took part and why the paper is important for cycling. Batur explains that it is a group of nutritionists who work in professional teams and at a university, and that the author team consists of several experts.

Batur states that it is not a single work but a series of **six to seven related papers** that together form a whole. He stresses that the paper is the result of joint effort by several experts from several teams, who each gave their input on individual topics. Although at some points there was confusion about the exact number and titles of the papers, Batur emphasizes that it is a series of publications that can be found and read.

As one of the important researchers he mentions an author who worked in sport for many years and collaborated with professional teams. Batur also states that one of the researchers was among the key people who made it possible to know certain figures related to carbohydrate intake today.

Batur particularly highlights the culture of critical thinking among scientists. In his words, papers are openly debated at congresses, and authors are not afraid to criticize each other's findings. As an example he cites the debate over a paper on relative energy deficiency in sport, which provoked heated reactions. Such a debate, he believes, shows that researchers are willing to have their results publicly examined, which, according to his experience, is not common in the Croatian context.

As the reason for the paper's importance, Batur states that it is a summary of existing knowledge that had been discussed for a long time but is now brought together in one place. The paper, in his words, is available in open access, which allows anyone interested to read and analyze it. For this reason, he concludes, the paper can serve for a long time as foundational literature for experts.

sections.subtitle: What the paper contains: from calorie expenditure to recovery and supplements
sections.screenshot_description: Table or chart from the paper showing calorie expenditure and speeds in races, alongside a visual representation of recovery.
sections.content:
Josip then asks what the paper covers. He mentions that in the paper he saw data on the average calorie expenditure of cyclists, but also a graphic showing the rise of average speeds in races over the years. He emphasizes that today's races, according to this data, are becoming ever faster, and as an example he cites speeds in the final stages which, as he says, were not possible earlier.

Batur replies that the topic of intake during riding is covered in detail. He explains that the paper shows different figures depending on the stage, terrain and intensity. He emphasizes that 120 grams of carbohydrates per hour is not a standard for every stage or every cyclist, but one example for certain conditions. There are, he adds, also examples where around 50 grams less per hour is consumed, especially on flat and shorter stages, while on mountain stages the situation is different.

Another important topic is the general context of nutrition, that is, periods of adaptation and periods of reduced intake, which depend on the level of preparation and the time of year. Batur stresses that the paper also covered the topic of injuries and preservation of athletes' health, which, as he says, is rarely discussed.

Josip mentions that professionals can have more than a hundred race days in a year, which Batur partly confirms, noting that in periods outside competition the importance of recovery is often neglected. The emphasis of the paper, in his words, is not only on recovery after an individual training session, but also on the weekly and monthly rhythm.

Finally, supplements are mentioned, that is, the difference between those that are pointless, those that can be dangerous and those that make sense. Batur notes that in the sports world sports nutrition is often reduced to manufactured gels and bars, and the paper also deals with differences in athletes' preferences.

According to Batur, the paper also covered areas that are rarely mentioned in sports discourse, such as the cooperation of nutritionists with chefs and kitchen staff in teams. One of the papers is devoted to how cooks translate nutritional calculations into dishes on the plate, which, as he points out, shows how comprehensive the paper is.

sections.subtitle: Carbohydrate intake during races and training: professionals versus recreational riders
sections.screenshot_description: Guest Luka Batur explains the differences in carbohydrate intake across different stages, while a comparison of professionals and recreational riders is shown on screen.
sections.content:
Batur emphasizes that recreational riders often compare themselves with professionals, which can be mistaken. In his opinion, many amateurs try to imitate top athletes without considering the context, guided by the impression that the more they consume, the faster they will reach the finish.

As the basis he explains the role of **carbohydrates as fuel** for endurance sports. In his words, the intensity and volume of training or racing are the main factors that determine the amount of intake. He adds that many athletes he follows do not eat enough carbohydrates, especially in endurance disciplines.

Batur explains that the differences between professionals and recreational riders are best seen through examples. On stages with higher altitude and longer rides the demands are considerably greater, so carbohydrate intake is more justified. In contrast, on shorter and flatter stages the needs are smaller.

For recreational riders who ride in a group, Batur gives an example that, according to him, he often sees. In a group of about twenty riders, only four to five riders actually pull, while the others take turns and save energy. He notes that some athletes after five hours of riding have an average power of around 150 watts, which is very close to the intensity of zone 2. The question, he says, is why such a rider would take very high amounts of carbohydrates if he were not actually pressing the pedals.

Batur also presents a contrast with practice in his own triathlon club, where recreational riders during weekend rides consume between zero and thirty grams of carbohydrates per hour. He recalls that even professionals, before muscle biopsies and precise measurement methods existed, got by with very small intakes, often only with cola.

Asked about the exact distribution, Batur estimates that 80 to 90 percent of recreational riders who ride three to five times a week, with one or two longer rides of two and a half to three and a half hours, would be satisfied with an intake that keeps them within reasonable limits. He adds that larger amounts are useful only for those who really maintain high intensity for a long time, such as marathon riders who, as he says, approach ninety percent of their threshold level during a race.

Josip notes that in his own experience, at a granfondo, he consumed less than professionals did, and Batur concludes that in that case it is more important to think about the goal of the ride than about numbers, unless the goal is to cover the section very quickly.

sections.subtitle: Example of a recreational rider at a granfondo: ease of intake and real needs
sections.screenshot_description: Josip describes his own example from a granfondo, with an illustration of a sandwich, an energy bar and a gel in a jersey pocket.
sections.content:
In the conversation Josip presents his own example from recreational riding. As a recreational rider who takes part in brevets, he says that for such rides he never calculates exact figures, but takes what he wants to eat and buys what he needs at that moment. He admits that his performance is nowhere near professional, but finds it interesting to think about how much he consumes and how this affects his riding.

Batur replies that accuracy is important only if our goal is to achieve a certain result. If the ride is not aimed at speed, then, he says, there is no need for a pencil and calculations. Still, he emphasizes that even in a recreational context one should be mindful and safe, because the goal is for riding with friends to be pleasant and to end without problems.

As a practical tip, Batur suggests adjusting intake to how one feels, with regular supply, for example one bar per hour or something sweeter in the bottle. He recommends planning intake in advance, especially on longer rides and brevets that can last up to two hundred kilometers, because otherwise it easily happens that one ends up with uneaten food or with depleted supplies.

Josip describes a specific situation from a demanding ride on Žumberak, where he first ate the sandwich he had brought, then an energy bar, a chocolate with gel and snacks. He admits that he was saving some supplies for emergencies and that because of this he started the climb hungry. When he finally ate the sandwich at the top, and then quickly took in more gels from his pocket, a pronounced digestive blockage occurred, although without any serious gastrointestinal problems.

Batur comments on this example as a classic situation in which a lack of planning leads to excessive carbohydrate intake in a short period, to which the body is not accustomed. He adds that it is important to adjust intake to the level of training and to get used to larger amounts gradually.

sections.subtitle: Gel, bar or chewing: why the choice matters on a demanding climb
sections.screenshot_description: Display of different forms of quick energy: liquid, gel, bar and gummy sweets, with a note about the correct timing of consumption.
sections.content:
Batur explains that practical problems with food during riding can be solved by choosing the right form. Gels and liquids are most suitable for more intense parts of the ride, because they are easily swallowed without chewing. Bars are, in his words, reserved for calmer parts of the route, because in a group or on a climb it is difficult to use one hand and chew.

When choosing solid food, Batur advises selecting products with little fat, protein and fiber. He explains that these three ingredients slow down stomach emptying and the transfer of glucose from the intestine into the bloodstream, so the fuel is used more slowly. That is why a bar is ideal if it is almost pure carbohydrate. Still, he points out that for athletes in a race or intense training it is not advisable to use protein bars, because protein is not a significant source of energy under these conditions, and total daily protein intake remains more important for recovery.

Batur also warns about the psychological and physiological aspect. During intense effort blood is redirected toward the muscles and the skin, so digestive functions are partly limited. That is why, he says, athletes should start taking carbohydrates earlier, while digestion is still functional, and not wait until fatigue and stress accumulate. Many recreational riders, as he notices, make the mistake of taking a gel only after a long time without food.

Josip adds that he himself felt discomfort when taking in food quickly, which coincides with Batur's explanation. Batur concludes that it is important to understand why such situations happen, because then it becomes clearer how to plan intake and avoid digestive troubles or sudden exhaustion.

sections.subtitle: Hypoglycemia and digestion under load: why the body rebels
sections.screenshot_description: Graphic showing the intestine and bloodstream with labels for carbohydrates and transporters, while a guest explains the physiology of digestion.
sections.content:
Batur explains that hypoglycemia, that is, a drop in blood sugar that can lead to fainting, happens rarely, but it can occur when an athlete neglects intake. For a recreational rider who rides with friends, the key goal is to safely reach the destination, and this is achieved through regular intake, adjusted to how one feels and to the plan.

During exertion, Batur says, blood is redirected toward the muscles and the heart, and the digestive system receives less blood. This means weaker contractions and mixing of food, and even weaker digestion. That is why he advises starting intake early, while the digestive system is still at full capacity, so that as much nutrients as possible enter the bloodstream in the first part of the ride.

Based on practical experience, Batur states that amateurs often wait as long as an hour and fifteen minutes before taking a gel. He admits that he sometimes did that himself, riding for fifteen to twenty minutes before taking a gel. As advice he suggests planning food before you feel fatigue, because then the body adapts more easily.

Josip adds that problems often arise because people do not remember to eat regularly, but only when it is too late. Batur agrees and emphasizes that the body can get used to larger intake, but that requires time and training.

sections.subtitle: How scientists arrived at the limit of 60 g glucose and 120 g carbohydrates per hour
sections.screenshot_description: Diagram of laboratory measurement: an athlete on a bike in the laboratory, breath measurement and an illustration of glucose and fructose transporters in the intestine.
sections.content:
Josip asks how scientists arrived at specific figures, such as 60 grams of glucose and 120 grams of carbohydrates per hour. Batur explains that this process was based on measurement in the laboratory, in which labeled carbon isotopes were used. The carbohydrate solution is labeled, the athlete consumes it during exertion, and then the amount of carbon dioxide in exhaled air is measured using calorimeters and similar devices.

Based on the difference between the amount ingested and the amount exhaled, researchers were able to conclude how much carbohydrate was actually utilized. Batur states that numerous tests were conducted to determine where the limit of utilization lies and how much the muscles can use at most.

One of the important conclusions was that there is a limit in the intestine. If glucose entered the blood directly, everything would be used quickly, but the transfer is limited by transporters in the intestinal wall. Batur explains that glucose is carried into the intestine by transporters that it is simpler to call types of “gates,” and that glucose cannot be absorbed faster than a certain rate.

Research has shown that the limit for glucose is around 60 grams per hour. It was later established that adding fructose activates other transporters, so the total amount can be raised and the available energy further increased. That is why a combination of glucose and fructose is recommended in practice, and 120 grams of carbohydrates per hour comes precisely from that combination.

Josip follows up with a question about the ratio of glucose and fructose and about substituting expensive gels with ordinary sugar. Batur replies that the research compared different types of sugar, including glucose, fructose and sucrose. While ordinary sugar contains approximately equal parts of glucose and fructose, fructose can cause greater digestive discomfort. Batur considers glucose to be slightly better, but he says that ordinary sugar is also a good and cheap choice for those who do not want to buy gels. He adds that honey, because of its price and practicality, is not the best solution for most athletes.

Finally, it is emphasized that the difference between professional and recreational athletes in this area is not in ability, but in needs and goals. Batur concludes that for most riders it is enough to follow the lower values, up to about 60 grams per hour, and that it is more important to eat regularly than to worry about exact ratios.

iterations.theme: Alternatives to gels, injury prevention through nutrition, practical examples and nutrition on long rides

sections.subtitle: Gels under the spotlight: sugar, glucose and honey as a cheaper alternative
sections.screenshot_description: Host Josip and guest Luka Batur in the studio, with a graphic on screen showing the ratio of glucose and fructose in sports gels and ordinary sugar.
sections.content:
In this part of the show the conversation shifts to a practical question: can athletes and recreational riders replace expensive gels and sports drinks with simpler foods. Josip relays a question from one viewer, who suggests ordinary sugar with a little salt, explaining that sucrose contains glucose and fructose in a 50:50 ratio and has no unnecessary flavorings or additives. A second viewer asks what Luka thinks about honey.

Luka Batur explains that researchers compared different sugars, including pure glucose, fructose, and even lactose, primarily because of the physical properties of sugar in the intestine. He points out that fructose can cause somewhat greater digestive discomfort, while glucose is better tolerated. Sucrose, that is, ordinary white sugar, can serve as a source of carbohydrates, but in that case the digestive effect is somewhat more pronounced.

As a practical example, Luka cites his own experiences from the beginning of his career, when he did not have money for expensive products and bought glucose at a drugstore, which he mixed himself. He would therefore, he says, give a slight preference to glucose, but emphasizes that sugar can also be used. About honey he has a clear position: he never used it to prepare a gel, because it is expensive, and the main problem is logistics, that is, how to package it and carry it during the ride.

**Key conclusions of the section on alternatives:**
- Glucose is absorbed in the intestine through its own transporters, and the limit identified by research is about 60 grams per hour.
- Adding fructose uses other transporters, which makes it possible to increase the total amount of carbohydrates reaching the bloodstream.
- The form and ratio of sources matter less for recreational riders who are not optimizing performance, but are interested in simply consuming something.
- Gummy sweets and similar simple products, according to Luka, are often sufficient in practice.

Josip concludes that the greatest advantage of gels is actually the packaging and quick absorption, that is, the ability to take in carbohydrates quickly without chewing, which is important when riding is intense. For a recreational rider like himself, he says, a gel can serve as first aid when his energy drops, rather than as a mandatory part of his diet.

sections.subtitle: Injury prevention through the plate: why an energy deficit is dangerous for athletes
sections.screenshot_description: Guest Luka Batur speaks to the camera, while a title on screen appears about injury prevention through nutrition and key terms: energy deficit, bones, immunity.

sections.subtitle: Example from a granfondo: from pasta to burgers and beer
sections.screenshot_description: Josip and Luka Batur sit at a table, while the screen shows a diagram of nutrition before and after a granfondo with the indicated carbohydrate intake.
sections.content:
Josip suggests that the theory be shown with a concrete example and asks Luka to describe how he ate before a recent granfondo. Luka explains that Saturday preceded the race on Sunday, and that on Friday and Saturday he deliberately increased his carbohydrate intake. This approach, he explains, is called glycogen supercompensation, and research shows that 24 hours is enough for its effect, but in practice it is more practical to do it over two days, because then it is easier to eat without overeating. On a satiety scale from seven to ten, he says, he felt he had reached about six to seven, which was comfortable.

The recommendation from research for very high needs is about 10 grams of carbohydrates per kilogram of body mass per day. For Luka, who weighs close to 90 kilograms, that would mean about 900 grams of pure carbohydrates. He admits that he probably did not fully achieve that, but he did increase his intake. For Friday and Saturday he describes meals rich in carbohydrates, with an emphasis on pasta, fruit and juices, while on the day before the race he avoided fats and fiber.

The race took place on Sunday and Luka rode it in about two hours. Before the start he drank about half a liter of coffee and ate several gummy sweets, which he used as a short-term boost. During the ride he consumed five to six gels, and he estimated his total intake at about 120 grams of carbohydrates per hour, or about 200 grams in total. However, in the last five to six kilometers he felt fatigue in his legs, which, as he admits, was not necessarily the result of too little intake, since he also made a tactical mistake and started pushing harder too early.

After the race recovery followed with bolognese and bread with potatoes and meat, plus forest fruits, and later cakes. Josip asked how important alcohol and pizza are after tiring days, and Luka emphasizes that one beer will probably not do harm, but that alcohol inhibits glycogen synthesis and can dehydrate, so for more serious goals it is not the best choice. He concludes that recreational riders often finish an intense training session or granfondo, and that in two to three days a new demanding training session awaits, which is why planning carbohydrate intake is crucial.

sections.subtitle: Muscles, protein and total daily intake: what really maintains muscle mass in cyclists
sections.screenshot_description: The screen shows a viewer's question about maintaining muscle mass, while Luka Batur explains daily protein needs with a graphic.
sections.content:
Josip relays a question from viewer Marin Milardović about how to most safely maintain muscle mass, that is, how to lose only fat tissue and not muscle tissue. Luka first separates two goals: maintaining and increasing muscle mass. He points out that not all cyclists are interested in large muscle mass, and that even most better cyclists look lean, because that suits them for climbing and the ratio of mass to power.

According to Luka, maintaining or growing muscle requires an adequate stimulus, which is usually strength training, which is the job of a kinesiologist. Nutrition alone, in his words, cannot replace such training. Still, proteins play an important role, but the total daily intake is key, not a special meal or intake during riding. There is no evidence that six to seven hours of riding without protein would lead to some severely negative consequences, unless this is part of an individual plan.

As an example, Luka cites a viewer who goes on a multi-day cycling tour. If he consumes part of his protein at breakfast, and the rest of the day's protein comes from dinner at a hotel or restaurant, that can be sufficient. Protein bars in such a situation will not necessarily do harm, but they are not necessary. For an athlete who wants to be at the top of the results the situation is different, so the needs may vary.

Luka adds that a loss of muscle mass after a month without specific strength training can be expected, even with sufficient protein, because muscles are not maintained by nutrition alone. As a recommendation he gives about 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body mass per day, which, according to research, is sufficient both for maintenance and even for muscle growth. He adds that given the amount of food consumed by cyclists, such figures are easy to reach.

Josip recalls that he himself was in contact with a viewer who plans a multi-day tour lasting five to seven days and asks whether he should do strength exercises. Luka admits that he is not a kinesiologist and does not want to give specific advice on strength training, but personally believes that in the short term there is no need to worry about losing a large amount of muscle mass, if strength training is not performed during that period.

sections.subtitle: Brevet and long rides: fats, sandwiches, magnesium and glycine
sections.screenshot_description: Josip reads a question from viewer Dejan, while the screen shows a sandwich with eggs and bacon and a water bottle.
sections.content:
Josip relays a question from viewer Dejan, who asks what to eat during and before brevet rides and how much and when to take magnesium. Dejan describes that during riding he most often eats sandwiches with eggs and bacon and various chocolate bars, and drinks water from a bottle.

Luka says that he himself would choose the egg and bacon sandwich as the last option. The reason is that fats and proteins slow down stomach emptying, and one does not want fuel to reach the bloodstream slowly. Although the body has enough fat even for the leanest athletes, it should not be additionally consumed during riding. He emphasizes that it is a pity when fats take up space that could be taken by carbohydrates. He adds a practical problem: such a sandwich easily spoils or becomes impractical to eat while riding.

As an alternative he suggests milder options such as a couple of slices of ham or light spread. The brevet format, he points out, is not the same as a race. If the goal is for the ride to be pleasant and to reach the finish without great stress, there is more room for preferences, but one should take care that the intake is not too burdensome for digestion.

As a personal example, Luka describes a bike ride from Zagreb to Šibenik three years ago. He did not have a special bag or much food with him, but used two strudels, half a liter of cola, carbohydrate bars and gummy sweets. From Gračac to Knin he had a more serious problem with dehydration, which is why he stresses the importance of fluid intake and does not recommend such an approach.

Asked about magnesium, Luka answers that he personally takes it in the evening, and that it is a myth that magnesium is lost through sweat in significant amounts, especially in sunny conditions. There is no recommendation for magnesium intake during activity. Most available products contain forms such as oxides and carbonates, which are poorly absorbed, so claims on packaging about large amounts often do not hold in practice. He additionally warns that there may also be an oxidative effect, so magnesium should not be taken either before or during activity.

Luka states that he himself takes glycine in the evening. Josip adds that he once took glycine during riding as a precaution and that it gives him the feeling that he feels better in his head. Luka replies that this is fine, but that according to available data there is no clear evidence that glycine during riding would have a serious effect on performance.

iterations.theme: Aligning nutrition with life obligations, carbohydrate sources on the ride, supplements, beetroot, caffeine and conclusion

sections.subtitle: How to align nutrition with work, obligations and hobbies?
sections.screenshot_description: Josip in the studio reads a viewer's question, while Luka Batur sits opposite him on a couch with a frame showing the chapter title “How to align nutrition with life obligations?”
sections.content:
Host Josip relays a question from viewer Dejan, who regularly follows the guest's posts on Instagram and wants to know how to align nutrition with all life obligations and hobbies, and how to deal with the feeling of needing something sweet. Guest Luka Batur emphasizes that he deals with such questions daily, both with athletes and with recreational riders, and that he regrets that the desire for sweets is often stigmatized.

Batur explains that in the context of sport, especially more intense sport, a large part of the desire for sweets is actually the result of a shortage of carbohydrates in the diet. As a typical example he cites the Sunday scenario of an average Croatian cyclist: after riding comes beer, then a barbecue or a stuffed meat specialty, and half a kilogram of meat is eaten, possibly with one potato, which is roughly 50 grams of carbohydrates. If a slice of bread is eaten along with that, and in the afternoon and evening a whole chocolate bar or Nutella by the spoonful follows, carbohydrate intake may be sufficient, but with an excess of fat and an overall unbalanced meal.

As a solution Batur recommends simple and affordable sources of carbohydrates: fruit, squeezed juice, bread, rice, pasta, potatoes, polenta and barley. He emphasizes that people should be encouraged to eat fruit, not to restrict themselves. He especially highlights the paradox that many people avoid carbohydrates in their diet, yet are not afraid of chocolate.

For people with more serious training, Batur advises planning carbohydrates according to the days. If a particularly demanding training session or race is ahead, for example a weekend with a long training session of four to five hours, it makes sense to increase carbohydrate intake in the preceding days. At the same time he stresses that nutrition can be organized at the household level, so that pasta, rice, lasagne or roast are planned on days when there is more training, while on calmer days one eats in a more balanced way.

Batur notes that for more concrete advice for Dejan, a few minutes of conversation would not be enough. He estimates that he would need about 45 minutes to get to know a person's everyday life and only then could turn their habits into practical advice.

sections.subtitle: Gels, bars or gummy sweets: what to choose during a ride?
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur explains a line of products on the table in front of him: gels, energy bars and gummy sweets, while Josip listens under the caption “Carbohydrate sources on the ride”.
sections.content:
Josip asks how many different sources of carbohydrates can be used during a ride, especially on a ride of about eight and a half hours, and whether it is better for the stomach to use two or three sources or more. Batur answers that different forms can be combined, liquids, gels, bars and gummy sweets, and that he even recommends it. Combining also helps avoid flavor saturation, which can arise when the same product is eaten for hours.

The guest emphasizes that the riding of recreational riders and races differ in their demands, so in the recreational context there is more room for preferences. Still, he recommends narrowing that room somewhat and trying different products during training. He advises trying different flavors, textures and brands, because some gels can be too sweet, sour, bitter or have an unpleasant smell.

As an example he cites one client who, using a systematic method without tables in Excel, recorded and ranked products by texture and flavor, and then narrowed the choice to several gels that he knew he could tolerate. Batur considers this approach simple and effective.

Josip adds that flavor and texture are individual matters and that people need to sense for themselves what suits them. He recommends trying new products on a relaxed ride, not just at the moment when it is important, so that one can see how the body reacts.

sections.subtitle: Lamb or veal: when nutrition becomes a matter of taste
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur smiles and shakes his head, while Josip holds a slip of paper with a viewer's question; the frame shows plates with fish on the table.
sections.content:
In a humorous tone, Josip asks the question of viewer Maki­ja: is spit-roasted lamb or veal under the bell better for cyclists. Josip himself says that lamb chops from the grill are “numero uno” for him, but Batur replies that the question was a joke and that he does not know how to give a firm answer.

Batur explains that in his region lamb and veal are not traditionally dominant foods, and he jokes that it is not clear how Dalmatia became a land of lamb and veal rather than fish. He reveals that his father is a fisherman, which is why he is subjective himself, and admits that he does not eat lamb or veal willingly either.

The guest adds that his wife Marija does not like chicken and that lately she hardly eats white meat at all. Josip concludes that the answer to the question is still that the best chops are the best, and the conversation returns to more practical topics.

sections.subtitle: Beetroot, nitrates, caffeine, beta-alanine and creatine: what is really useful?
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur with notes in his hand explains the role of nitrates, while the screen shows the subtitle “Beetroot and supplements” and a glass of beetroot juice.
sections.content:
The conversation moves on to supplements. Josip notes that many in amateur cycling ask about beetroot, which is popular in athletes' diets. Batur explains that nitrates from beetroot help with economy of work, meaning that a greater output can be achieved with the same amount of oxygen. Beetroot juice can enable faster work or greater overall work under equal conditions.

The guest states that research shows the effect may be smaller in athletes who are already well trained, because they have probably reached a certain plateau of adaptations. Still, beetroot juice can help with better performance efficiency, and Batur himself consumed it for several days before an important race. For success at a half Ironman he plans to consume it during the week before the race.

For optimal use the guest mentions that research refers to half a liter of juice per day for three to four days, and even up to seven days before the main event. Such a regimen is not practical for most amateurs, and supplements can also be expensive.

About caffeine Batur says that it can reduce the perception of fatigue and that most people recommend it, but not in the afternoon hours so that it does not affect sleep. Josip asks whether it makes sense for athletes to “clean out” caffeine during winter. Batur answers that according to research such a procedure is not necessary, because people who usually drink coffee remain sensitive to caffeine. As a useful practice he cites avoiding caffeine in later afternoon hours, since caffeine has a half-life of three to four hours. He recommends that caffeine sources, such as coffee or energy drinks, be reduced at the latest nine hours before sleep.

For creatine Batur says that it can help with recovery and glycogen synthesis, and that it is most useful for teams that need greater strength and explosiveness, such as sprint teams or cyclists in disciplines with frequent sudden accelerations. For recreational riders its importance is smaller. He mentions beta-alanine as a supplement that helps neutralize hydrogen ions associated with fatigue during high-intensity intervals, while he describes sodium bicarbonate as an agent that can cause serious digestive problems.

sections.subtitle: Conclusion: do not copy professionals, but build sustainable nutrition
sections.screenshot_description: Josip and Luka Batur sit in the studio, Josip asks for a summary, and the lower banner shows the title “Conclusion of the UCI paper and end of the podcast.”
sections.content:
Josip asks for a summary of the whole conversation. Batur briefly answers that amateurs should not imitate professionals in carbohydrate intake per hour, especially not those of half a kilogram per hour in the hope that they will thereby become better. The key message is that nutrition during the rest of the day, including breakfast, the afternoon meal and dinner, plays a decisive role in recovery.

The guest emphasizes that total daily intake, quantity and quality of food are the key factors, and that high intake during riding is by itself not an indicator of quality nutrition. When it comes to supplements, or to injuries and infections, the most important thing is to ensure sufficient energy. Antioxidants in tablet form are not a priority, and doses above physiological levels are not recommended either.

Batur also mentions the example of juices that athletes drink after stages in the Tour, stating that the idea is to recover quickly for the next day, but that excessive amounts of antioxidants can interfere with adaptations to training.

At the end of the conversation the guest comments on alcohol. He reminds that one beer will probably not be a problem, but that alcohol can slow glycogen synthesis and lead to dehydration. For those who want to recover quickly and effectively, consuming alcohol is not recommended, especially in the first hours after a serious training session or race.

Josip concludes the conversation by announcing that the link to the paper will be in the podcast description, encourages viewers to comment, and suggests that the guest in the future record nutrition videos for the channel or open his own channel.
